title: Check your understanding: Writing Effective Commit Messages

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of writing effective commit messages?
options: A useful commit subject states the change clearly and specifically. A body can capture why the change was needed, the chosen trade-off or relevant issue; avoid vague subjects that do not help future readers understand history.
Git automatically backs up every file, including ignored and untracked files, to a remote.
The operation grants every contributor write access to the hosted repository.
questions.answer_key: A useful commit subject states the change clearly and specifically. A body can capture why the change was needed, the chosen trade-off or relevant issue; avoid vague subjects that do not help future readers understand history.
questions.explanation: A useful commit subject states the change clearly and specifically. A body can capture why the change was needed, the chosen trade-off or relevant issue; avoid vague subjects that do not help future readers understand history.

questions.prompt: Which command is the most direct starting point for this lesson’s example?
questions.explanation: Use `git log -1 --format=%B` as the first inspection/action in the example, and then verify the result with the companion checks in the lesson.

questions.prompt: Which is the safest general practice when working with writing effective commit messages?
options: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
Run the most destructive option first; the reflog guarantees every file can always be recovered.
Assume the local command also changed the remote and satisfied all hosting-platform policies.
questions.answer_key: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
questions.explanation: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
